content.content: # Actions, resources, and condition keys for AWS services Each AWS service can define API operations, actions, resources, and condition context keys for use in IAM policies. This topic describes how the elements provided for each service are documented. Each topic consists of tables that provide the list of available operations, actions, resources, and condition keys. ## The operations table The **Operations** table lists the API operations defined by the service and maps each one to the IAM actions that authorize it. A single operation can authorize more than one IAM action. Some services do not yet have an operations table. This does not mean there are no operations for that service. This table does not yet include actions that downstream services authorize through [forward access sessions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_forward_access_sessions.html). + The **Operation** column lists the name of the API operation. When an operation authorizes multiple actions, the operation name spans the rows for all of its authorized actions. + The **IAM action** column lists each IAM action authorized by the operation, in the form `service:ActionName`. When the action belongs to the same service as the operation, the entry links to that action's row in the **Actions** table on the same page. When the action belongs to a different service, the entry links to that service's authorization reference page. + The **Condition key** and **Possible value(s)** columns list only the condition keys that this operation sets to a fixed, known value when it authorizes this action, along with the value it sets. This is not the full set of condition keys that may be available during authorization. The keys shown are the ones with values determined statically by the API itself. For the full set of condition keys supported by the action, see the [**Actions** table](#actions_table) and the [**Condition keys** table](#context_keys_table) on the same page. + The **Access level** column shows the access level classification of the authorized action. For more information about access levels, see [Understanding access level summaries within policy summaries](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_understand-policy-summary-access-level-summaries.html). ## The actions table The **Actions** table lists all the actions that you can use in an IAM policy statement's `Action` element. Some services include permission-only actions that don't directly correspond to an API operation. These actions are listed in a separate **Permission-only actions** table on the same page. Use these tables to determine which actions you can use in an IAM policy. For more information about the `Action`, `Resource`, or `Condition` elements, see [IAM JSON policy elements reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements.html). The **Actions** and **Description** table columns are self-descriptive. + The **Access level** column describes how the action is classified (List, Read, Write, Permissions management, or Tagging). This classification can help you understand the level of access that an action grants when you use it in a policy. For more information about access levels, see [Understanding access level summaries within policy summaries](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_understand-policy-summary-access-level-summaries.html). + The **Resource types** column indicates whether the action supports resource-level permissions. If the column is empty, then the action does not support resource-level permissions and you must specify all resources ("\*") in your policy. If the column includes a resource type, then you can specify the resource ARN in the `Resource` element of your policy. For more information about that resource, refer to that row in the **Resource types** table. All actions and resources that are included in one statement must be compatible with each other. If you specify a resource that is not valid for the action, any request to use that action fails, and the statement's `Effect` does not apply. Required resources are indicated in the table with an asterisk (\*). If you specify a resource-level permission ARN in a statement using this action, then it must be of this type. Some actions support multiple resource types. If the resource type is optional (not indicated as required), then you can choose to use one but not the other. + The **Condition keys** column includes keys that you can specify in a policy statement's `Condition` element. Condition keys might be supported with an action, or with an action and a specific resource. Pay close attention to whether the key is in the same row as a specific resource type. This table does not include global condition keys that are available for any action or under unrelated circumstances. For more information about global condition keys, see [AWS global condition keys](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html). ## The resource types table The **Resource types** table lists all the resource types that you can specify as an ARN in the `Resource` policy element. Not every resource type can be specified with every action. Some resource types work with only certain actions. For more information about the `Resource` element, see [IAM JSON policy elements: Resource](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_resource.html). + The **ARN** column specifies the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) format that you must use to reference resources of this type. The portions that are preceded by a $ must be replaced by the actual values for your scenario. For example, if you see `$user-name` in an ARN, you must replace that string with either the actual user's name or a [policy variable](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_variables.html) that contains a user's name. For more information about ARNs, see [IAM ARNs](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_identifiers.html#identifiers-arns). + The **Condition keys** column specifies condition context keys that you can include in an IAM policy statement only when both this resource and a supporting action from the table above are included in the statement. ## The condition keys table The **condition keys** table lists all of the condition keys that you can use in an IAM policy statement's `Condition` element. Not every key can be specified with every action or resource. Certain keys only work with certain types of actions and resources. For more information about the `Condition` element, see [IAM JSON policy elements: Condition](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition.html). + The **Type** column specifies the data type of the condition key. This data type determines which [condition operators](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition_operators.html) you can use to compare values in the request with the values in the policy statement. You must use an operator that is appropriate for the data type. If you use an incorrect operator, then the match always fails and the policy statement never applies. If the **Type** column specifies "ArrayOf.." one of the simple types, then you must use [multivalued set operators](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-single-vs-multi-valued-context-keys.html#reference_policies_condition-multi-valued-context-keys) in your policies. Use the `ForAllValues` prefix to specify that **all** values in the request must match a value in the policy statement. Use the `ForAnyValue` prefix to specify that **at least one** value in the request matches one of the values in the policy statement. **Topics** + [Operations table](#operations_table) + [Actions - **Attachment points:** Yes. Deny policies attach to an organization, folder, or project, and lower-level resources inherit them.
- **Exception principals:** Yes. The optional `exceptionPrincipals` field exempts listed principals from a rule, even if they belong to a denied group.
- **Denial conditions on resource tags:** Yes, but they're limited. Conditions are optional, and they "only recognize resource tag functions." The rule applies when the condition is true or can't be evaluated.

- **Limits:** Each resource can have up to 500 deny policies, and those policies can contain 500 deny rules in total.

The page documents the Feed Management API for creating, running, and managing data feeds that send logs to Google Security Operations.

- **Deprecation:** The Backstory API is deprecated and will be discontinued on July 20, 2027. Use the Chronicle API to manage feeds and accounts instead.
- **Authentication:** Requests use a Google Developer Service Account credential with the scope `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/chronicle-backstory`.
- **Rate limits:** Create, Get, List, Update, and Delete Feed are each limited to 1 query per second. Exceeding this returns HTTP 429, so clients should rate-limit.
- **Core operations:** Create, Get, List, Update, Delete, Enable, and Disable Feed, plus `fetchFeedServiceAccount` for Cloud Storage feeds.
- **Feed states:** `ACTIVE`, `INACTIVE`, `IN_PROGRESS`, `COMPLETED`, and `FAILED`. Failed feeds include a `failure_details` block.
- **Credential validation:** For third-party API feeds, invalid credentials block feed creation.
- **Feed source types:** Third-party API, Pub/Sub push, Cloud Storage (V2 and event-driven), Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon S3 (V2), Amazon SQS (V2), Azure Blob Storage (V2), Azure Event Hub, HTTP(S), and webhook. Several v1 connectors are deprecated, with discontinuation on March 15, 2027.
- **Ingestion limits:** A single log line can't exceed 4 MB. Deduplication happens at the batch level, not the log level.
- **Latency:** Third-party API feeds are forward-moving and can't backfill. Microsoft feeds have a mandatory 5-minute lag. Bucket-based feeds depend on pull frequency.
- **IP allowlisting:** V2 feeds need the Storage Transfer Service ranges (`ipranges.json`). Third-party APIs need `goog.json`.
- **Regional endpoints:** Endpoints are provided for many regions, such as `backstory.googleapis.com` for the US multi-region.

Links: [{"title":"Securing Environmental Variables","url":"https://forum.serverless.com/t/securing-environmental-variables/6398"},{"title":"DEV Community","url":"https://dev.to/eoinsha/3-ways-to-read-ssm-parameters-4555"},{"title":"• Documentation","url":"https://www.serverless.com/framework/docs/guides/variables/aws/ssm"},{"title":"#  How to Reference Parameter Store Values in CloudFormation","url":"https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-12-parameter-store-cloudformation/markdown"},{"title":"dynamic references ssm","url":"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/dynamic-references-ssm.md"},{"title":"oneuptime.com","url":"https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-02-12-parameter-store-cloudformation/view"},{"title":"bref.sh","url":"https://bref.sh/docs/environment/variables"}]

The search supports the core concern: a Serverless Framework `${ssm:}` value can end up as plaintext in the generated CloudFormation template. The sources are mixed in age and authority, so treat the forum report as anecdotal.

- **Plaintext in the template:** A Serverless forum user reported that encrypted SSM parameters referenced with `${ssm:secret~true}` were compiled to plaintext in both the CloudFormation template and the Lambda environment variables. They are compiled to plain text and placed in the Cloudformation template as well as in the Lambda Environmental variables. The post is undated and I couldn't confirm the current behavior.
- **How resolution works:** The Serverless docs say every ${ssm:} reference reads one parameter with the GetParameter API, and the decrypted value is what the variable holds (the serverless variable will contain the decrypted value of the secret). Resolution happens before a command runs, and throttled calls are retried up to 10 times by default (the Framework resolves all variables concurrently before a command runs).
- **Build-time vs. deploy-time:** One article classes `${ssm:}` as a build-time read, which means the build environment needs the credentials and the parameter must exist even when you're only building (it also requires you to ensure that your build environment has the right credentials). It also notes that CloudFormation's native parameter types are more stable and validate at deploy time (CloudFormation syntax tends to be more stable, ensures deploy-time validation).
- **Native CloudFormation alternatives:** A dynamic reference, `{{resolve:ssm:...}}`, works only for `String` or `StringList` parameters (access values from parameters of type String or StringList in Parameter Store). Parameter types like `AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<String>` resolve the latest value at deploy time without a version number (CloudFormation will then retrieve the latest version of the parameter value from Parameter Store).
- **Practical guidance:** A Bref guide advises against putting secrets in `serverless.yml` and suggests injecting them at deploy time for simplicity or at runtime for better security (either at deployment time (simplest) or at runtime (more secure)).

Bottom line: values resolved through `${ssm:}` are generally expected to land in the deployed stack's configuration in plaintext. For secrets, the safer pattern is to fetch them at runtime or use a secure mechanism, and to verify the synthesized template for your Framework version.

**AWS CloudTrail via S3/SQS**
- The setup involves creating a trail that writes to S3, then wiring an SNS topic to an SQS queue. The SNS subscription needs raw message delivery turned on so the parser gets the raw CloudTrail payload (the SQS subscription is created from the SNS topic, and raw message delivery must be enabled for Google SecOps to receive the raw payload).
- The IAM policy needs sqs:DeleteMessage, since without that permission Google SecOps can't delete messages from the queue.
- Deprecation: the v1 S3, SQS, and Azure Blob feed types are slated for shutdown on March 15, 2027 (the v1 feed types for GOOGLE_CLOUD_STORAGE, AMAZON_S3, AMAZON_SQS, and AZURE_BLOBSTORE are deprecated and will be discontinued on March 15, 2027). The V2 variants are the ones to plan around.

**Google Cloud Audit Logs and Kubernetes audit**
- Direct ingestion uses Cloud Logging filters to forward logs to Google SecOps, with Cloud Audit Logs among the supported types (direct ingestion is the most common method for Google Cloud telemetry and uses Cloud Logging filters to forward logs).

The alternative is a webhook feed (Google Cloud Storage V2 is recommended, with a webhook as the other option for pushing payloads to Google SecOps in real time).
- The SecOps service account needs Storage Object Viewer on the bucket.

**Data model, detection, and SOAR**
- Parsers convert raw logs into UDM, which downstream features such as rules and UDM search depend on (parsers convert customer logs into UDM, and downstream systems use it for rules and UDM search).
- YARA-L 2.0 is the detection language. Recent additions include cross joins in multi-stage queries (cross joins are now available in YARA-L 2.0 multi-stage queries) and the re.capture_all function (re.capture_all is available in Rules, Search, and Dashboards).

- Oversized events are dropped: a batch over 8.2 MB drops all its UDM events, and a single UDM event over 500 KB is dropped.

- **Persistence:** Once set, the value stays in requests for the rest of the role session, including role chaining. The docs say it can't be changed after it's set. (After a source identity is set, it is present in requests for any AWS action taken during the role session. The value that is set persists when a role is used to assume another role through the AWS CLI or AWS API, known as role chaining.)
- **Permission requirement:** Roles connected to an IdP need the `sts:SetSourceIdentity` permission in their trust policies, or the `AssumeRole*` operation fails. AWS suggests a separate IdP instance for passing source identity if you don't want to edit every role's trust policy. (If you don't want to update the role trust policy for each role, you can use a separate IdP instance for passing source identity.)
- **CLI usage:** You pass the value explicitly with the `--source-identity` flag on `aws sts assume-role`. (aws sts assume-role --role-arn arn:aws:iam::<AccountId>:role/Developer_Role --role-session-name Audit --source-identity Admin)
- **Enforcement:** Trust policies can require a specific source identity value through an `sts:SourceIdentity` condition. (The AWS administrator can also add a condition statement for the sts:SourceIdentity key to a role's trust policy, that would require the workforce identity to set their source identity when they assume the role.)

Transitive tags are set with `--transitive-tag-keys`, persist through role chaining, and override matching role tags after the trust policy is evaluated. Limits: at most 50 tags, key 128 characters, value 256 characters. You can't pass session tags from the console.
